*HDS MSc · Module 3 · the R version of this exercise; the web page is at <https://inflamuob.github.io/HDS_M3/day5/day5-01-regression-metrics.html>.*

*Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time. Keep it in the folder that holds your `data` folder. Cells with `______` are blanks for you to fill in.*

On Day 3 you fitted a straight line to predict glucose and measured its error
with a loss function. A model is only useful if it also predicts **people it has
not seen**. In this exercise we fit a model on the training rows, predict both
the training and the test rows, and compare the errors. The comparison tells us
whether the model is **overfitting** (much better on training than on test) or
**underfitting** (similar on both, but poor on both).

Suppose we believe that the relationship between glucose and age is not a
straight line but a **cubic**:

$$\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{age} + \beta_2\,\text{age}^2 + \beta_3\,\text{age}^3$$

> **The plots are for looking at**
>
> The code for every plot is included, so that you can run it and see the figure. You are not expected to write it yourself.

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 4)     # show four significant figures in tables
```

The data are in [`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv). We split the
750 people into a training set and a test set, as in earlier exercises: 80% for
training and 20% held back as the test set, 600 and 150 people. `set.seed(42)`
makes the random split the same every time.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(glucose, mass, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

dim(diabetes)
dim(train)
dim(test)
```

750 people: 600 for training (80%) and 150 for testing (20%).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — A cubic model as a pre-processing step

To fit a cubic we do not need a new kind of model. We create new columns from
age (its square and its cube) and fit an ordinary linear regression on them.
Creating new columns from old ones is **feature engineering**, so in tidymodels
it belongs in the **recipe**, alongside the other pre-processing steps you met
on Day 2. `step_poly()` adds the polynomial columns:

```{r}
cubic_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

cubic_rec <- recipe(glucose ~ age, data = train) |>
  step_poly(age, degree = 3)
```

Look at what the recipe does to the data. `prep()` works out the transformation
from the training rows and `bake(new_data = NULL)` applies it to them:

```{r}
cubic_rec |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)
```

Age has been replaced by three columns, `age_poly_1` to `age_poly_3`. They are
not simply age, age² and age³: `step_poly()` makes **orthogonal** polynomials,
rescaled versions that carry the same information but are uncorrelated with
each other, which keeps the computer's arithmetic accurate. The fitted curve is
exactly the same cubic.

Now put the model and the recipe together in a **workflow** and fit it on the
training rows:

```{r}
cubic_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(cubic_spec) |>
  add_recipe(cubic_rec)

model_cubic <- cubic_wf |>
  fit(data = train)

tidy(model_cubic)
```

The four coefficients belong to the orthogonal columns, so they are hard to read
on their own, and they differ from the ones you would get from the raw powers of
age, which Python uses. On the same data the **predictions** are identical either
way, and the predictions are what we evaluate.

Here is the fitted cubic on top of the training data:

```{r}
age_grid <- data.frame(age = 21:81)
curve <- augment(model_cubic, age_grid)

ggplot(train, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(y = .pred), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "Cubic fit of glucose on age, training rows")
```

> **Learning points**
>
> - A polynomial model is a linear regression on new columns made from the predictor.
> - Making those columns is pre-processing, so it lives in the recipe (R) or the pipeline (Python), together with the model.
> - R's `step_poly()` uses orthogonal polynomials and Python's `PolynomialFeatures()` uses raw powers: different coefficients, identical predictions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Predictions on the training and the test rows

We want to know whether the model **generalises**: does it predict new people as
well as the people it was fitted on? So we predict both sets. `predict()` gives
a column `.pred`:

```{r}
predict(model_cubic, new_data = train) |>
  head()
```

It is easier to keep the predictions next to the data. `augment()` does that in
one step: it adds the prediction `.pred` and the residual `.resid` (observed
minus predicted) to each row. Do it for the training rows and the test rows:

```{r}
train_preds <- augment(model_cubic, new_data = train)
test_preds  <- augment(model_cubic, new_data = test)

head(test_preds)
```

The first test person is 28 years old with a glucose of 194, and the model
predicts 125.9 for them: an error of 68.1 mg/dL, a person the model gets badly
wrong.

```{r}
both_sets <- bind_rows(train_preds |> mutate(set = "train (600)"),
                       test_preds  |> mutate(set = "test (150)")) |>
  mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("train (600)", "test (150)")))   # train first

ggplot(both_sets, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .pred), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ set) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "The same fitted cubic, on the training and the test rows")
```

> **Learning points**
>
> - The model is fitted on the training rows only; the test rows are used for predicting, never for fitting.
> - Keep the predictions next to the data: `augment()` in R, a new column in Python.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Measuring the error, by hand and with a package

For a regression model the error of one person is $y_i - \hat{y}_i$, the observed
glucose minus the predicted glucose. Three summaries of these errors are used
everywhere; you met them as loss functions on Day 3:

$$\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \qquad
\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}} \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i - \hat{y}_i|$$

RMSE and MAE are in the units of the outcome, mg/dL, so they can be read as
"the typical size of an error". MSE is in squared units. Compute all three on the
training rows, one step at a time:

```{r}
train_preds |>
  mutate(error = glucose - .pred) |>
  summarise(MSE  = mean(error^2),
            RMSE = sqrt(MSE),
            MAE  = mean(abs(error)))
```

On the training rows the typical error is about 30 mg/dL (RMSE 29.98, MAE
24.13). Now do the same for the **test** rows:

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
test_preds |>
  mutate(error = ______) |>
  summarise(MSE  = mean(error^2),
            RMSE = ______,
            MAE  = mean(abs(error)))
```

> **Stuck?**
>
> Copy the training cell and change `train_preds` to `test_preds`. The error is
> the observed glucose minus the prediction `.pred`, and RMSE is the square root
> of MSE.

You will compute these metrics for every model you build, so packages already
do it. In tidymodels they come from **yardstick**: each metric takes the data,
the column with the truth and the column with the prediction. `metric_set()`
bundles several metrics into one function:

```{r}
rmse(train_preds, truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)

reg_metrics <- metric_set(rmse, mae)
reg_metrics(train_preds, truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
```

The same numbers as by hand. Check the test rows with the package as well:

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
reg_metrics(______, truth = glucose, estimate = ______)
```

**Question!** The model is about as good on the test rows as on the training
rows. Is it overfitting? Is it a good model? A typical error of 30 mg/dL, when
most glucose values lie between 80 and 180, is large. What would you try next?

The errors are similar on both sets, so there is no sign of **overfitting**. But
they are large on both, which is **underfitting**: age alone cannot capture what
drives a person's glucose, whatever the shape of the curve. The natural next step
is to add predictors, not to make the curve more flexible.

> **Learning points**
>
> - MSE, RMSE and MAE summarise the errors $y_i - \hat{y}_i$; RMSE and MAE are in the units of the outcome.
> - Always compute them on both the training and the test rows, and compare.
> - Much better on training than on test: overfitting. Similar but poor on both: underfitting.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — More flexible is not more accurate

Was the cubic the right choice? Fit polynomials of degree 1 (a straight line) up
to 8, and record the training and test RMSE of each. The code is the same as in
Part 1 with a different `degree`, repeated in a loop:

```{r}
degree_results <- data.frame()

for (d in 1:8) {
  poly_wf <- workflow() |>
    add_model(linear_reg()) |>
    add_recipe(recipe(glucose ~ age, data = train) |>
                 step_poly(age, degree = d))
  poly_fit <- poly_wf |>
    fit(data = train)

  train_rmse <- augment(poly_fit, new_data = train) |>
    rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
  test_rmse <- augment(poly_fit, new_data = test) |>
    rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)

  degree_results <- bind_rows(degree_results,
                              data.frame(degree     = d,
                                     train_rmse = train_rmse$.estimate,
                                     test_rmse  = test_rmse$.estimate))
}

degree_results
```

```{r}
degree_results |>
  pivot_longer(c(train_rmse, test_rmse), names_to = "set", values_to = "RMSE") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = degree, y = RMSE, colour = set)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Degree of the polynomial", y = "RMSE (mg/dL)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Training error keeps falling; test error does not")
```

The training RMSE falls with every extra degree, from 30.53 for the straight line
to 29.88 for degree 8: a more flexible curve can always follow the training
points more closely. The test RMSE does not follow. It is lowest at degree 6
(30.44) and rises again after that, to 30.68 at degree 8. The extra flexibility is spent on
the noise of these particular 600 people, which does not repeat in new people.
With 600 people and a single predictor the effect is small; with fewer people
or more flexible models it can be very large.

**Question!** Which degree would you choose, and on which data did you base the
choice? (Look again at the Stretch below.)

> **Learning points**
>
> - Training error always improves as a model becomes more flexible, so it cannot be used to choose how flexible a model should be.
> - Test error stops improving, and starts to get worse, once the model fits noise: that is overfitting.
